problem.title: Machines outnumber humans — but most lack strong identities

items.title: Certificate Sprawl
items.desc: Thousands of X.509 certificates managed manually across teams. Expired certs cause outages; forgotten certs create silent attack surfaces. No single team owns the full lifecycle.

items.title: Hardcoded Credentials
items.desc: API keys, passwords, and tokens embedded in source code, container images, and config files. A single leaked repository can expose your entire infrastructure to attackers.

items.title: No Lifecycle Management
items.desc: Service credentials are created but never rotated. Certificates expire without warning. Decommissioned workloads leave long-lived secrets behind, invisible to security teams.

problem.solution_title: Cryptographic identity for every workload — automated from birth to death
problem.solution_desc: SPIFFE/SPIRE, automated X.509 certificate issuance, and mutual TLS give every machine a verifiable identity. Issued automatically at workload start, rotated continuously (default: 1 hour), and revoked instantly upon decommission — with no human in the loop.

architecture.title: From workload start to secure mTLS in 7 steps
step_titles: Workload starts — SPIRE Agent detects via Workload API
Agent attests its own identity to the SPIRE Server
SPIRE Server validates workload via K8s API
SPIRE Server issues SVID (X.509 cert) to the workload
Workload initiates mTLS connection to Service B
Service B validates SVID against the SPIFFE trust bundle
Secure mTLS channel established — SVID auto-rotates every hour
flow: Kubernetes projects a service account token into the pod filesystem. The SPIRE Agent, running as a DaemonSet on every node, detects the new workload through the SPIFFE Workload API and begins the attestation process.

The SPIRE Agent collects workload selector data (pod UID, service account, namespace) and forwards a node attestation request to the SPIRE Server. The Agent itself must first prove the node's identity before vouching for workloads.

The SPIRE Server calls the Kubernetes API Server to verify the pod metadata matches the expected selectors defined in the registration entry. This binds the workload's identity to its K8s attributes — no static configuration in the workload needed.

Once verified, the SPIRE Server signs a short-lived X.509 SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document) and delivers it to the workload via the Agent. The SVID contains the workload's SPIFFE ID (e.g. spiffe://trust-domain/ns/prod/sa/payments) in the SAN field.
The workload uses the SVID as a TLS client certificate to initiate a mutual TLS handshake with Service B. No API keys or passwords are passed — the certificate is the credential.

Service B validates the workload's SVID against the shared SPIFFE trust bundle. Both sides verify each other's certificates, establishing mutual authentication. The connection is rejected if the SVID is expired or the SPIFFE ID doesn't match the registered policy.

The mTLS channel is now live. Both workloads hold valid SVIDs. The SPIRE Agent automatically rotates the SVID before expiry (default: 1 hour), so credentials are always fresh and revocation is near-instant — just stop issuing new SVIDs.

whatis.title: What is Machine Identity?
whatis.subtitle: A machine identity is a cryptographic credential that proves who — or what — a digital entity is, without human involvement.
whatis.types_title: Types of machines that need identities

types.label: Containers & Pods
types.desc: Every pod in Kubernetes needs a verifiable identity to authenticate with other services, APIs, and secret stores — without embedding credentials.

types.label: Virtual Machines
types.desc: Cloud VMs running applications or agents must prove their identity to cloud APIs, vaults, and inter-service communications.

types.label: CI/CD Pipelines
types.desc: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and GitLab CI runners need identities to access secrets, registries, and deployment targets — without storing long-lived tokens.

types.label: IoT & Edge Devices
types.desc: Embedded devices and edge nodes require lightweight certificates to authenticate with cloud backends and maintain secure firmware update channels.

types.label: Serverless Functions
types.desc: Lambda, Cloud Functions, and Azure Functions need short-lived identity tokens to call downstream APIs without static API keys.

types.label: Service Accounts
types.desc: Kubernetes service accounts, AWS IAM roles, and GCP service accounts form the IAM layer for machine-to-machine access control.

threats.title: What happens when machines lack strong identities
threats.subtitle: The top attack vectors that exploit weak or absent machine identities — with real-world impact.

items.title: Credential Theft
items.desc: Attackers scan GitHub, Docker Hub, and CI logs for exposed API keys, tokens, and certificates. Once obtained, these credentials grant lateral movement across cloud environments with no trace of how the attacker got in.
items.example: 2020: GitHub scraped for secrets → 2M+ exposed API keys in public repos

items.title: Certificate Expiry Outages
items.desc: Manually managed certificates expire without warning. A single expired cert in a service mesh can cascade into a production outage affecting thousands of users — and the blast radius grows with microservice count.
items.example: 2021: Spotify outage due to expired internal TLS certificate

items.title: Zombie Identities
items.desc: Decommissioned workloads leave behind service accounts, API keys, and certificates that remain valid for months. Attackers compromise abandoned infrastructure and pivot into live environments using orphaned credentials.
items.example: 42% of service accounts in enterprises are never deprovisioned (IDIRA 2023)

items.title: Lateral Movement via Machine Credentials
items.desc: Once an attacker compromises one workload, hardcoded credentials to databases, APIs, and secret stores enable rapid lateral movement. Machine credentials are the primary vehicle for privilege escalation in cloud breaches.
items.example: SolarWinds supply chain: attackers moved laterally for 9 months using service credentials

items.title: Supply Chain Identity Injection
items.desc: Malicious packages and compromised build systems inject backdoor credentials into container images. Without image signing and workload attestation, there is no way to verify that a running workload is what it claims to be.
items.example: Codecov breach: bash uploader modified to exfiltrate environment variables

items.title: Man-in-the-Middle on Service Mesh
items.desc: Without mutual TLS between microservices, an attacker on the same network can intercept traffic, replay requests, or inject malicious responses. Plain HTTP between services is the norm in many Kubernetes clusters.
items.example: CNCF survey: only 36% of K8s clusters enforce mTLS between services

certificates.title: Certificates are the bedrock of machine identity
certificates.subtitle: X.509 certificates provide cryptographically verifiable identity for machines. Understanding the lifecycle — from issuance to revocation — is essential to securing any modern infrastructure.

lifecycle.label: Generate
lifecycle.desc: Create a private key and CSR (Certificate Signing Request) for the workload. The private key never leaves the workload.

lifecycle.label: Issue
lifecycle.desc: The Certificate Authority signs the CSR, binding the public key to the workload's identity (subject name, SANs, validity period).

lifecycle.label: Distribute
lifecycle.desc: The signed certificate is delivered securely to the workload. In SPIFFE/SPIRE, the Agent handles this over a local Unix socket.

lifecycle.label: Use
lifecycle.desc: The workload presents the certificate in TLS handshakes. mTLS uses both sides' certificates for mutual authentication.

lifecycle.label: Rotate
lifecycle.desc: Before expiry, the workload requests a new certificate. SPIRE automates rotation (default: renew at 50% of lifetime).

lifecycle.label: Revoke
lifecycle.desc: On decommission or compromise, the certificate is added to the CRL or OCSP is queried. SPIFFE handles this by simply not issuing new SVIDs.

spiffe.title: Universal workload identity — without secrets in config
spiffe.subtitle: SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone) is a CNCF standard that gives every workload a cryptographically verifiable identity — without any secrets in environment variables, config files, or Kubernetes secrets.
spiffe.svid_desc: A SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document (SVID) is either an X.509 certificate or a JWT that carries the workload's SPIFFE ID in the Subject Alternative Name field. The SPIFFE ID is a URI of the form spiffe://trust-domain/path — making identity portable across clouds and clusters.

benefits.title: No secrets in workloads
benefits.desc: Workloads receive SVIDs via a local Unix socket. No credentials are passed through environment variables, Kubernetes secrets, or config files.

benefits.title: Short-lived by default
benefits.desc: SVIDs have a 1-hour lifetime by default. Compromise of a cert gives an attacker < 1 hour before it expires and is never renewed.

benefits.title: Platform agnostic
benefits.desc: Works on bare metal, VMs, containers, and serverless. Attestation plugins support AWS, GCP, Azure, Docker, and Kubernetes.

benefits.title: Automatic rotation
benefits.desc: The SPIRE Agent monitors SVID expiry and transparently renews certificates without any action from the workload.

spiffe.attestation_desc: SPIRE verifies workload identity by inspecting kernel-level data — the calling process's UID, GID, binary SHA-256, pod labels, or Kubernetes service account. This prevents a workload from lying about its own identity.

mtls.title: Both sides prove who they are — no passwords
mtls.subtitle: Standard TLS verifies the server to the client. Mutual TLS (mTLS) adds client authentication — both parties present X.509 certificates, creating a cryptographic handshake that replaces passwords, API keys, and network-level trust.

handshake.label: Client Hello
handshake.desc: Client sends supported cipher suites and TLS version.

handshake.label: Server Certificate
handshake.desc: Server sends its X.509 certificate. Client verifies against trust bundle.

handshake.label: Client Certificate
handshake.desc: Server requests client certificate. Client sends its SVID.

handshake.label: Certificate Verify
handshake.desc: Both sides verify each other's certs against the SPIFFE trust bundle.

handshake.label: Session Keys
handshake.desc: Both derive symmetric session keys. Encrypted channel established.

handshake.label: Mutual Auth Done
handshake.desc: Both identities are verified. Traffic flows over an encrypted, mutually authenticated channel.

zerotrust.title: Never trust, always verify — for every machine
zerotrust.subtitle: Zero Trust replaces network-perimeter security with identity-based access. Machine identity is the core primitive: every workload must prove who it is before accessing any resource, regardless of where it runs.

principles.title: Verify Explicitly
principles.desc: Authenticate every workload, every time. No implicit trust based on network location, IP address, or VLAN membership.

principles.title: Least Privilege Access
principles.desc: Each machine gets only the permissions it needs for its current task. Short-lived credentials enforce this — you cannot hoard access.

principles.title: Assume Breach
principles.desc: Design as if an attacker is already inside. mTLS, short-lived SVIDs, and continuous attestation limit blast radius when something goes wrong.

zerotrust.stack_title: The Zero Trust machine identity stack

stack.desc: Issues short-lived X.509 SVIDs to every workload automatically.
Every service-to-service call is mutually authenticated using the SVID.
Policy engine validates the caller's SPIFFE ID against the resource's access policy.
Workload presents SVID to secret store to retrieve dynamic credentials — no static secrets.
Every certificate issuance, rotation, and revocation event is logged and auditable.

kubernetes.title: Workload identity in Kubernetes clusters
kubernetes.subtitle: Kubernetes provides several identity primitives — but not all of them are strong. Here's what each one does, and how to harden them with SPIFFE/SPIRE.

primitives.name: Service Account Tokens
primitives.desc: Kubernetes automatically mounts a JWT into every pod at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. Since K8s 1.21, these are bound tokens with a 1-hour TTL. Use projected service account tokens for OIDC federation.

primitives.name: SPIFFE/SPIRE SVIDs
primitives.desc: SPIRE Agent runs as a DaemonSet and issues X.509 SVIDs to pods via the SPIFFE Workload API. SVIDs are attested using the K8s API — the pod cannot lie about its service account, namespace, or labels.

primitives.name: cert-manager Certificates
primitives.desc: cert-manager automates X.509 certificate lifecycle in-cluster. Use with the SPIFFE issuer or your own CA to give every pod a valid TLS certificate for mTLS without manual cert management.

primitives.name: Workload Identity Federation
primitives.desc: Federate K8s service account tokens with AWS IAM, GCP Workload Identity, or Azure Managed Identity. Pods get cloud-provider IAM roles without storing cloud credentials in Kubernetes secrets.

hardening: Disable automounting of service account tokens on pods that don't need them (automountServiceAccountToken: false)
Use projected service account tokens with audience and expiry set, not the legacy long-lived tokens
Deploy SPIRE Agent as a DaemonSet and register all sensitive workloads with entry selectors
Enable mTLS for all east-west traffic using Istio, Linkerd, or SPIFFE direct integration
Federate SPIFFE trust domains across clusters with SPIRE federation bundles
Block access to the instance metadata API from pods that don't need cloud credentials
Audit all ServiceAccount → ClusterRoleBinding relationships quarterly
Use OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno to enforce SPIFFE workload registration before deployment

certmgr.title: Certificate
certmgr.subtitle: Managing X.509 certificates at scale requires automation, strong policies, and continuous monitoring. Learn the full lifecycle — from discovery to revocation — and the tools that keep it under control.

certmgr.lifecycle_subtitle: A certificate's life spans six stages, each with its own risks if left unmanaged. Automation at every stage is the difference between a 3 AM outage and a seamless rotation.
certmgr.stage_discovery_desc: Find all certificates across your infrastructure. Unknown certs are the biggest source of expiry outages. Scan networks, cloud APIs, and code repositories.
certmgr.stage_issuance_desc: Request and sign certificates through a trusted CA. Automate CSR generation, validation, and signing to eliminate manual steps and human error.
certmgr.stage_deployment_desc: Deliver the signed certificate to the workload securely. cert-manager, Vault, and SPIRE handle deployment directly to Kubernetes pods and services.
certmgr.stage_monitoring_desc: Track expiry dates, usage, and anomalies across all certificates in real time. Alert on certs expiring in under 30 days and detect unexpected changes.
certmgr.stage_renewal_desc: Renew certificates before expiry — automatically. Best practice is to renew at 50-75% of lifetime, so there is always a valid cert even if renewal fails once.
certmgr.stage_revocation_desc: Invalidate compromised or decommissioned certificates immediately via CRL or OCSP. In SPIFFE, revocation is instant: simply stop issuing new SVIDs.
certmgr.practices_subtitle: Security teams that follow these practices reduce certificate-related incidents by over 80%. Each maps to a specific NIST control.
certmgr.practice_automate_desc: Manual certificate management does not scale. Use cert-manager, Vault PKI, or a CLM platform to handle issuance, renewal, and revocation without human intervention.
certmgr.practice_shortlived_desc: Certificates with a 90-day or shorter lifetime limit the window of exposure if a private key is compromised. ACME (Let's Encrypt) enforces 90 days; SPIFFE defaults to 1 hour.
certmgr.practice_inventory_desc: You cannot protect what you cannot see. Keep a real-time inventory of every certificate, its expiry date, issuing CA, and owning team. Scan continuously for shadow certificates.
certmgr.practice_policy_desc: Define and enforce policies for key size (RSA 2048+, ECDSA P-256+), allowed SANs, maximum validity, and permitted CAs. Reject any certificate request that violates policy.
certmgr.practice_ctlogs_desc: Certificate Transparency (CT) logs provide a public, append-only record of every certificate issued by a CA. Monitor CT logs to detect misissued or unauthorized certificates for your domains.
certmgr.practice_keyprotect_desc: Private keys must never leave the workload unencrypted. Use HSMs or TPMs for high-value keys. For Kubernetes, use sealed secrets or Vault for key storage — never plain Kubernetes secrets.
certmgr.practice_alerts_desc: Alert at 30, 14, and 7 days before expiry. A cert that expires without renewal takes down every service that depends on it. Alerts are the last line of defense when automation fails.
certmgr.tools_subtitle: Purpose-built tools that automate certificate lifecycle management across cloud, Kubernetes, and enterprise environments.
certmgr.tool_certmanager: Kubernetes-native certificate controller. Integrates with Let's Encrypt, HashiCorp Vault, and custom CAs to automate issuance and renewal for any workload in the cluster.
certmgr.tool_vault: HashiCorp Vault PKI secrets engine issues dynamic, short-lived certificates with configurable TTLs. Supports CRL, OCSP, and intermediate CA chaining for full enterprise PKI.
certmgr.tool_letsencrypt: Free, automated CA using the ACME protocol. Issues 90-day DV certificates and drives the adoption of short-lived certs across the internet. Ideal for public-facing services.
certmgr.tool_venafi: Enterprise CLM platform providing centralized policy, inventory, and automation across all machine identity types. Integrates with every major CA, cloud provider, and DevOps toolchain.
certmgr.pitfall_expiry_title: Ignoring expiry until it is too late
certmgr.pitfall_expiry_desc: Certificate expiry is the most common cause of unplanned outages. Without automated alerts and renewal, a cert that expires on a Sunday brings down production at the worst possible time.
certmgr.pitfall_wildcard_desc: A wildcard like *.example.com covers all subdomains but a single private key compromise exposes every service. Prefer per-service certificates with automation to manage scale.
certmgr.pitfall_gitkeys_desc: Committing a private key to a Git repository exposes it permanently — even if deleted later, it remains in history. Use secret scanning and pre-commit hooks to prevent this.
certmgr.pitfall_manual_desc: A ticket-based renewal process is a reliability risk. When the team is on vacation or the on-call engineer misses the alert, the cert expires. Automate renewal so humans are only in the loop for policy changes.
